PYQ • Q1, Q4

1Bioinformatics: from data to discovery

A DNA sequence is a string of letters. Bioinformatics turns that string into an answer: which gene is it, what does it do, and why might its mutation matter?

The two definitions you should be able to write

Bioinformatics is an interdisciplinary field that develops and applies computational tools to collect, store, organize, retrieve, analyse and interpret biological data. It combines biology, computer science, mathematics and statistics. Typical data include nucleotide and protein sequences, macromolecular structures, gene expression and pathways.

Computational biology uses computational, mathematical and statistical models to understand biological systems and test biological hypotheses. Examples include modelling an epidemic, simulating a gene regulatory network, and predicting protein structure.

AspectBioinformatics emphasisComputational biology emphasis
Main taskManaging and analysing biological informationExplaining or predicting biological behaviour
ExampleBuild a sequence database; search it with BLASTModel how a regulatory network responds to stress
RelationshipBoth fields overlap extensivelyA distinction in emphasis, not a rigid boundary
Biological question→Experiment / public data→Storage & QC→Analysis→Interpretation→Validation

Data → information → knowledge

Data are recorded observations: a sequence, a read count, or a patient measurement. Information is data given context, such as “gene X has four times as many normalized reads after heat stress”. Knowledge connects this information with evidence and a biological explanation. Metadata are data about data: organism, tissue, treatment, replicate, instrument, protocol and processing version.

Imagine rice plants grown at 28 °C and treated at 45 °C. Raw reads alone cannot tell you which plants were treated. Metadata make the comparison meaningful. A large amount of data with wrong sample labels can produce a confident but wrong conclusion.

Why biology needs computers

  • High-throughput technologies generate more data than can be examined manually.
  • Databases enable storage, sharing, cross-referencing and reproducible retrieval.
  • Algorithms detect sequence similarity, patterns, variants and differential expression.
  • Statistical models separate biological signals from random variation and technical bias.
  • Visualization helps turn complex results into testable biological hypotheses.

Bio-data science (BDS)

The Goh and Wong paper brings together biology + computer science + mathematics/statistics. Biological knowledge must guide computation. Genes in a pathway and proteins in a complex are related; treating every measurement as an isolated number can miss the biology.

Analytics levelQuestionBiological example
DescriptiveWhat happened?Plot gene-expression levels
DiagnosticWhy might it have happened?Identify pathways associated with stress
PredictiveWhat may happen next?Predict a disease subtype from molecular data
PrescriptiveWhat action should be considered?Compare candidate interventions using a validated model
Exam-ready opening

Bioinformatics integrates biological knowledge with computational and statistical approaches for the management and interpretation of biological information. Follow the definition with two data types and one application.

Remember

Data volume does not replace experimental design. Association is evidence for a hypothesis; it is not automatically proof of causation.

Quick check · answer before revealing

1. Which task best illustrates computational biology?
Modelling a biological system illustrates the computational-biology emphasis; the fields overlap.
2. Which is metadata?
Metadata describe how and from where the observations were obtained.

PYQ • Q1(b), Q5

2History & landmark projects

Learn history as a chain of problems solved: determine sequences → store them → compare them → sequence genomes → measure entire systems.

1953

DNA double helix
Watson and Crick proposed the double-helix model using key experimental evidence, including X-ray work by Franklin and Wilkins.

1955

Insulin protein sequence
Sanger’s work showed that a protein has a definite amino-acid sequence.

1958 / 1970

Central dogma
Crick proposed and later clarified the rules of sequential information transfer.

1965

Dayhoff’s Atlas
Atlas of Protein Sequence and Structure helped establish systematic sequence comparison and the foundation for PIR.

1970

Needleman–Wunsch
Dynamic programming made optimal global sequence alignment possible.

1971

Protein Data Bank
A public archive made experimental macromolecular structures reusable.

1977

DNA sequencing
Sanger chain termination and Maxam–Gilbert chemical sequencing enabled direct sequence determination.

1981–1982

Local alignment & sequence archives
Smith–Waterman local alignment (1981); GenBank became a major public nucleotide archive (1982).

1986 / 1988

Protein curation & NCBI
Swiss-Prot began in 1986; NCBI was established in 1988.

1990

BLAST & HGP
Fast local sequence searches and the launch of the Human Genome Project changed scale.

1995

Bacterial genomics & microarrays
The Haemophilus influenzae genome and expression microarrays expanded genome-wide research.

2001 / 2003

Human genome
Draft genome papers appeared in 2001; HGP completion was announced in April 2003.

2005 onward

Next-generation sequencing
Massively parallel sequencing lowered cost per base and increased throughput.

2008 onward

RNA-Seq and integrated omics
Sequencing-based transcriptomics, then single-cell, spatial and multiomics methods revealed cellular diversity.

Human Genome Project (HGP)

An international effort carried out from 1990 to 2003 to determine a human reference genome sequence, map genes, improve sequencing/computational methods, and make the data publicly available. It established infrastructure for comparative genomics, variant analysis and disease-gene research. The human genome contains approximately 3 billion base pairs.

The HGP reference was a major achievement, but it was not a complete account of every person’s genome or of all gene functions. Much repetitive sequence remained unresolved; later telomere-to-telomere and pangenome efforts extended the reference.

ENCODE

ENCyclopedia Of DNA Elements, launched in 2003, seeks to identify functional elements in the human genome: protein-coding and noncoding transcripts, promoters, enhancers, transcription-factor binding regions and chromatin features. HGP asks “what is the sequence?”; ENCODE asks “which elements are active, where, and in what context?” Biochemical activity does not by itself establish that every active base is essential or evolutionarily functional.

GenomeIndia

A DBT-supported project initiated in 2020 to catalogue genetic variation across India’s diverse populations. The initial phase sequenced about 10,000 individuals from 99 communities; the data resource was dedicated to researchers in January 2025. It supports population genetics, interpretation of variants and future precision-medicine research. Population representation, informed consent and protection of genomic data are central concerns.

Dates that older notes can mix up

PDB was established in 1971. GenBank officially began in 1982, following earlier sequence-collection work. Swiss-Prot began in 1986. Some uploaded notes give other dates; use the clarified dates in this guide.

Five-mark structure

Write a one-sentence introduction, then 6–8 chronological milestones with a phrase explaining each advance, and end with the transition to high-throughput omics.

Quick check · answer before revealing

1. Which pairing is correct?
HGP ran from 1990 to 2003. ENCODE investigates genomic functional elements.
2. Dayhoff is especially associated with…
Her Atlas helped establish systematic protein-sequence analysis.

Core concept

3Information flow & systems biology

A cell is a connected system. Measuring one gene can help, but the phenotype depends on interactions among genes, proteins, metabolites and the environment.

Systems theory studies how interacting components give rise to the behaviour of the whole. Emergent properties arise from interactions and cannot be understood by considering isolated parts alone. Systems biology combines experiments, omics, networks and models to understand these properties.

Molecules→Organelles→Cells→Tissues→Organs→Organism→Population→Community→Ecosystem

Bottom-up: a genetic variant changes protein activity, which alters metabolism and contributes to a phenotype. Top-down: temperature, nutrients or disease change signalling and gene expression. Environmental selection can change variant frequencies across generations; it does not intentionally rewrite DNA to meet an organism’s needs.

The central dogma

Arrows show transfer of sequence information, not merely regulation.

Replication: DNA → DNA

Semiconservative synthesis gives each daughter DNA one parental and one new strand. Helicase separates strands, single-strand binding proteins stabilize them, primase makes primers, DNA polymerase extends 5′→3′, and ligase joins fragments. The leading strand is continuous; the lagging strand uses Okazaki fragments.

Transcription: DNA → RNA

RNA polymerase uses a DNA template to synthesize RNA 5′→3′. In eukaryotes, pre-mRNA typically undergoes 5′ capping, intron removal by splicing and polyadenylation. Not every RNA becomes a protein.

Translation: RNA → protein

The ribosome reads mRNA codons. tRNAs pair their anticodons with codons and deliver amino acids. Initiation usually begins at AUG; elongation forms peptide bonds; a stop codon recruits termination factors. Codon means three nucleotides; a protein is a chain of amino acids.

Special transfers and the precise rule

Reverse transcription uses an RNA template to make cDNA, as in retroviruses and conventional RNA-Seq library construction. Reverse transcriptase has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity; RNase H removes RNA from an RNA–DNA hybrid and a second DNA strand can be produced. RNA replication uses RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, often encoded by the virus.

Crick’s actual restriction

Detailed residue-by-residue sequence information does not flow from protein back into nucleic acid or into another protein sequence. RNA → DNA is compatible with this rule. A protein regulating transcription, or a prion influencing protein folding, is not transfer of an amino-acid sequence back into a nucleotide sequence.

The omics layers

LayerWhat is measured?Useful question
GenomicsDNA sequence and variantsWhat could the cell do?
EpigenomicsDNA methylation and chromatin stateWhich regions are accessible or regulated?
TranscriptomicsRNA species and abundanceWhich genes are expressed now?
ProteomicsProteins, abundance and modificationsWhich functional molecules are present?
MetabolomicsSmall moleculesWhat biochemical state or output is observed?
InteractomicsMolecular interactionsWhich components work together?
Phenomics / ionomicsPhenotypes / elemental compositionWhat traits or mineral patterns emerge?

mRNA abundance and protein abundance need not match: translation rates, degradation, time delays and post-translational regulation all matter. This is why combining omics can provide a fuller picture.

Quick check · answer before revealing

1. Which transfer is compatible with Crick’s rule?
Reverse transcription does not transfer sequence information out of protein.
2. An emergent property arises primarily from…
Systems theory explains whole-system properties through interactions.
Close the notes. Retrieve it.Draw the five valid arrows. Explain why reverse transcription is not a violation of Crick’s central dogma.

PYQ • Q2

4Biological databases & their classification

A database is a computerized archive that organizes related data so information can be retrieved easily. Retrieval is called firing a query in your teacher’s slides.

A database management system (DBMS) is the software that creates, maintains and provides access to the database. It controls redundancy, security, integrity, concurrent access, backup and recovery, and supports queries. A relational database represents data as tables (relations), connected through keys.

A record and its cross-references

Accession / identifier→Sequence or structure→Annotation→Evidence & references→Links to other records

An accession number identifies a database record. A version tells you which revision you used. Annotation describes features such as a coding sequence, function, domain, organism and evidence. Cross-referencing links an entity to corresponding records elsewhere. A gene symbol can change or be ambiguous; stable identifiers and species context reduce mistakes.

Axis 1: primary, secondary and composite

ClassPrincipleExamples and what they contain
Primary / archivalOriginal experimental sequence or structural data submitted by researchersGenBank, EMBL/ENA, DDBJ: nucleotide sequences; PDB: experimentally determined macromolecular structures
Secondary / derivedInterpretation, analysis or classification of primary dataPROSITE: motifs/patterns; Pfam: protein families/domains; SCOP and CATH: structure classification
Composite / integratedCombine or link information from multiple resourcesInterPro integrates protein family/domain/signature resources; GeneCards integrates human-gene information; UniProt integrates protein sequence and knowledge resources
Match the course’s classification

The slides list Swiss-Prot, TrEMBL and PIR among primary protein-sequence resources. Keep that convention if asked to classify as taught, but describe Swiss-Prot as manually curated and TrEMBL as computationally annotated. “Primary”, “curated” and “integrated” describe different aspects and are not always mutually exclusive.

Axis 2: classify by type of data

Data typeExamplesWhat you retrieve
Nucleotide sequencesGenBank, ENA (historically EMBL), DDBJDNA/RNA sequence records and features
Protein sequencesUniProtKB: Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL; PIRAmino-acid sequence, function, domains and modifications
Sequence patterns / motifsPROSITE, Pfam, InterProConserved signatures, protein families and functional sites
3D macromolecular structurePDB; NDB for nucleic-acid structuresAtomic coordinates and experimental structure information
Gene expressionGEO, ArrayExpress; SRA/ENA for raw sequence readsExpression studies, sample metadata, processed values or raw reads
PathwaysKEGG, ReactomeMetabolic or signalling pathways and participating molecules
Variation / reference sequencesdbSNP; RefSeqVariant records; curated/reference genomic, RNA and protein sequences
Organism / disease-specificTAIR, FlyBase, SGD, MGD/MGI, PlasmoDB, OMIMModel-organism genetics or human gene–phenotype information

Axis 3: availability and accessibility

Your slides distinguish publicly available without restrictions; available with copyright; accessible but not downloadable; academic but not freely available; and proprietary/commercial, possibly with academic access. Access policy is independent of data type. Publicly visible information can still have licence conditions. Sensitive human data may require controlled access.

The major resources in teacher language

  • INSDC: International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration: GenBank + ENA/EMBL + DDBJ. Data exchange makes submissions available through partner resources.
  • Swiss-Prot: high-quality, manually reviewed annotation, including protein function, domains, variants and post-translational modifications.
  • TrEMBL: “Translated EMBL”; automatically annotated, unreviewed protein records supplementing the curated set.
  • UniProt: Universal Protein Resource; sequence and functional information, identifier mapping and analysis links.
  • PDB: Protein Data Bank; a structure archive. It includes protein and nucleic-acid macromolecular structures, not only protein sequences.
  • TAIR: The Arabidopsis Information Resource; genes, gene products, expression, markers and plant research resources.
  • PlasmoDB: functional genomics of Plasmodium parasites.
  • KEGG: Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes; pathways, genes and biological systems.
  • OMIM: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man; human genes and genetic phenotypes.

Read a sequence record

LOCUS        example sequence summary
ACCESSION    stable record identifier
VERSION      identifier.sequence-version
SOURCE       organism
REFERENCE    supporting publication
FEATURES     gene / CDS / exon annotations
ORIGIN       nucleotide sequence

FASTA is simpler: a header beginning with > followed by sequence. It does not include per-base sequencing quality scores.

How to answer Q2

Define data (1 mark), define database (1 mark), then name three classification axes and explain types with examples (3 marks). Primary/secondary alone is not the whole classification scheme.

5NCBI, EBI & PubMed searching

NCBI and EBI are organizations. Entrez is the integrated retrieval system. PubMed is a literature-search resource. BLAST is a sequence-similarity search tool.

TermExpansion / role
NCBINational Center for Biotechnology Information; part of the US National Library of Medicine, NIH
EBIEuropean Bioinformatics Institute; generally called EMBL-EBI
EntrezNCBI’s integrated search and retrieval system across literature, genes, sequences, structures and related data
PubMedSearchable biomedical literature citations and abstracts; includes MEDLINE and other records
PMCPubMed Central: a full-text archive. PubMed results do not all contain free full text.
MeSHMedical Subject Headings: NLM’s controlled vocabulary for indexing biomedical topics

Advanced literature searching: the logic

  1. Break the question into concepts. Example: breast cancer + BRCA1 + review.
  2. Add synonyms within a concept with OR. This broadens retrieval.
  3. Join distinct concepts with AND. This narrows retrieval.
  4. Use field tags. [tiab] searches title/abstract; [au] author; [mh] MeSH; [dp] publication date.
  5. Use the Advanced Search Builder and history. Combine earlier sets, e.g. #1 AND #2; inspect Search Details to see PubMed’s translation.
  6. Refine with filters. Date, article type, language, species and other filters can help. Index-dependent filters may exclude newly added or incompletely indexed records.
  7. Read and save results. Evaluate relevance and evidence, then export citations or save a search through My NCBI.
FeatureExampleMeaning / caution
ANDBRCA1 AND cancerBoth concepts must be represented
ORcancer OR neoplasmEither synonym; broadens a set
NOTcancer NOT miceExcludes records; can remove relevant papers
Parentheses(asthma OR wheeze) AND childGroups alternatives before combining concepts
Field restrictionBRCA1[tiab]Targets a field rather than unrestricted searching
MeSH + keywords"Breast Neoplasms"[mh] OR "breast cancer"[tiab]Combines indexed concepts with text in newer records
Date range2020/01/01:2025/12/31[dp]Limits publication dates
Truncationtherap*Finds variants of a word; broad stems can add noise
Phrase searching"breast cancer"[tiab]Targets a phrase; quoted/tagged searches change automatic mapping behaviour

A complete example

("Breast Neoplasms"[mh] OR "breast cancer"[tiab])
AND BRCA1[tiab]
AND review[pt]

Unqualified PubMed terms can undergo Automatic Term Mapping (ATM) to subjects, journal names or authors. Explicit field tags and phrase restrictions change how mapping works. MeSH improves conceptual retrieval, but keywords capture records that have not yet received MeSH indexing.

Build a query offline

This builder teaches syntax; it does not fetch live PubMed results.



A 3-mark answer
Name Advanced Search Builder/history, Boolean operators, field tags, MeSH and filters; demonstrate a query. Explaining just “type a keyword in PubMed” misses advanced searching.

6Tools, algorithms & applications


For the five-tool question, write tool → what it does → one specific application. A list of names without functions will be incomplete.


Tool / algorithmPrinciple or functionSpecific application
BLASTBasic Local Alignment Search Tool; heuristic local sequence-similarity searchIdentify a candidate homolog of an unknown gene/protein in a database
ClustalW / Clustal OmegaMultiple sequence alignmentFind conserved residues or motifs across a protein family
MEGAMolecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis; evolutionary analysis and phylogenetic reconstructionBuild a phylogenetic tree from homologous aligned sequences
HISAT2Splice-aware alignment of sequencing readsMap RNA-Seq reads to a reference genome, including exon-junction reads
DESeq2Count-based statistical testing with a negative-binomial modelFind genes differentially expressed between treated and control samples
FastQC / MultiQCRead-quality report / aggregation of QC reportsCheck base quality, adapter content and consistency across samples
fastpRead filtering and adapter trimmingRemove low-quality reads and adapters before alignment
featureCounts / HTSeq-countAssign aligned reads/fragments to annotated featuresProduce a gene-by-sample count matrix from BAM and GTF files
CytoscapeNetwork visualization and analysisExplore protein-interaction or gene-regulatory networks
DAVID / GSEAFunctional annotation/enrichment / ranked-list gene-set enrichmentDetermine whether pathways or gene sets are overrepresented or coordinated


Sequence alignment: global versus local
Global alignment aligns sequences across their full lengths, appropriate for broadly similar sequences of comparable length. Needleman–Wunsch uses dynamic programming to find an optimal global alignment under a scoring scheme. Local alignment finds the best matching region; Smith–Waterman is optimal under its scoring scheme. BLAST is faster through a heuristic search and extension strategy, trading exhaustive optimality for practical database searching.


Sequence A: ACCTGACCT
Sequence B: AC-TGACCT
                 ↑ gap accommodates an insertion/deletion
Scoring rewards matches and penalizes mismatches/gaps. Protein alignments often use PAM or BLOSUM substitution matrices. A BLAST E-value estimates the number of chance matches with an equal or better score expected in that search. A smaller E-value indicates stronger evidence against chance similarity; database size and query length affect it.


Avoid the homology trap
Homology means common evolutionary ancestry, not a percentage. Write “80% sequence identity”, rather than “80% homology”. Similarity can support a homology hypothesis, but function still needs evidence.


BLAST variants
VariantQuery → target
blastnNucleotide → nucleotide
blastpProtein → protein
blastxTranslated nucleotide query → protein database
tblastnProtein → translated nucleotide database
tblastxTranslated nucleotide query → translated nucleotide database


Phylogeny and visualization
Align homologous sequences before comparing them. A tree summarizes an evolutionary hypothesis, not simply a ranking of visual similarity. Bootstrap support estimates stability under resampling; it does not prove that a branch is correct. In networks, nodes represent genes/proteins/metabolites and edges represent interactions or relationships. A co-expression edge is a statistical association, not necessarily direct physical binding.


Five safe choices for Q4
BLAST, ClustalW, MEGA, HISAT2 and DESeq2 cover sequence search, alignment, evolution, read mapping and expression analysis. Use the functions in the table as five numbered points.

2. A smaller BLAST E-value generally means…
E-value estimates expected chance matches at that score or better.
3. The correct wording is…
Homology denotes an evolutionary relationship, not a percentage.

PYQ • Q5(b)
7DNA sequencing, NGS & family genomics


Sequencing determines the order of bases. NGS determines many sequences in parallel, making genome-scale studies practical.


First-generation sequencing
Sanger chain-termination sequencing uses a template, primer, DNA polymerase, ordinary dNTPs and chain-terminating ddNTPs. A ddNTP lacks a 3′-OH group, so extension stops when it is incorporated. Fragments of different lengths are separated by capillary electrophoresis; labelled terminal bases reveal the sequence. It produces relatively long, accurate reads but low throughput compared with NGS.
Maxam–Gilbert sequencing uses base-specific chemical cleavage of labelled DNA; hazardous reagents and complexity limited its routine adoption.


Next-generation sequencing
NGS refers to high-throughput methods that sequence large numbers of DNA fragments in parallel. Second-generation methods typically involve library preparation and amplification followed by massively parallel short-read sequencing.


DNA / cDNA→Fragment + adapters→Library→Clusters / templates→Parallel sequencing→Reads→Bioinformatics


Illumina sequencing by synthesis
  1. Adapter-ligated fragments bind complementary oligonucleotides on a flow cell.
  2. Clonal amplification forms clusters (the details vary by instrument).
  3. Fluorescent reversible-terminator nucleotides are incorporated during cycles.
  4. Images record the incorporated base; the block and dye are removed before the next cycle.
  5. Base calling produces sequences with quality scores.


Watch sequencing cycles
A simplified one-template model: each click reads one more base.
 


TechnologyCore principleStrength / limitation
IlluminaSequencing by synthesis; commonly short readsHigh throughput and accurate base calls; repetitive regions and complete isoforms can be difficult
454 (historical)Pyrosequencing detects signals linked to nucleotide incorporationImportant early NGS platform; homopolymer-length errors
Ion TorrentDetects hydrogen ions released on incorporationElectronic detection; homopolymer challenges
PacBio SMRTSingle-molecule real-time sequencingLong reads; repeated observations in HiFi improve accuracy
Oxford NanoporeElectrical-current changes as molecules pass through poresLong reads, portable options and direct RNA; accuracy depends on chemistry and analysis
Older platform numbers are snapshots
Read lengths, run times and error rates in the slides describe particular instruments and protocols. Do not memorize them as universal values. Long reads can resolve repeats and full isoforms; modern high-accuracy long-read methods differ from older noisy single-pass reads.


Single-end versus paired-end
Single-end reads one end of a library fragment. Paired-end reads both ends of the same fragment. The known pairing improves mapping, structural-variant interpretation and transcript analysis. The two reads are not the same as sequencing both complementary strands; paired-end data require more sequencing and processing.


Genome strategies and a useful formula
ApproachUseMain trade-off
Whole-genome sequencing (WGS)Coding, noncoding and structural variationBroadest scope; more data and interpretation
Whole-exome sequencing (WES)Protein-coding exons enriched by captureLess data/cost; misses most noncoding variation and can have uneven capture
Targeted panelSelected disease-associated genesFocused coverage; cannot discover variants outside the panel
Approximate genome coverage = N × L / G, where N is the number of reads, L their length and G genome size. Example: 100 million 150-base reads for a 3-billion-base genome gives average 5× coverage. For 100 million read pairs, each 150 bases at both ends, the nominal total is 10×. Real coverage is uneven.


Family-based variant analysis
Phenotype & pedigree→WGS / WES / panel→QC & mapping→Variant calling→Filtering & annotation→Segregation→Validation
Compare affected and unaffected relatives. A dominant variant may track affected family members; a recessive disease may involve biallelic variants; an X-linked pattern must be evaluated with sex and inheritance; a de novo variant may occur in a child and be absent from the sampled parents. Filter by read quality, frequency, predicted effect and inheritance, then assess clinical and experimental evidence. Rare does not automatically mean pathogenic; predicted damage is not a diagnosis. Complex traits involve multiple loci and environmental contributions.
Challenges include repeats, mapping bias, structural variants, missing coverage, uncertain significance, incidental findings and genomic privacy. Confirm important candidates with appropriate validation.
Quick check · answer before revealing
1. Why does a ddNTP terminate a DNA chain?
Without a 3′-OH the chain cannot be extended in the ordinary polymerase reaction.
2. Paired-end sequencing means…
The relationship between the read pair helps mapping.
3. A rare variant is automatically pathogenic.
Rarity is one evidence type; pathogenicity needs additional evidence.

PYQ • Q5(c)
8Measuring expression & noncoding RNAs


A genome is comparatively stable; a transcriptome changes with tissue, time and condition. Expression studies ask which RNA molecules are present and how their abundance differs.


Transcriptome: the complete set of RNA transcripts in a cell, tissue or organism under a specified condition and time. It includes coding and noncoding RNA, although an mRNA-enriched experiment measures only part of it.


MethodPrincipleWhat to remember
Northern blottingSeparate RNA by size → transfer to membrane → hybridize a labelled probeDetects transcript size and relative abundance; requires a suitable probe
Ribonuclease protection assayAntisense probe hybridizes to RNA; RNase removes unhybridized RNAProtected fragments support sensitive detection and quantification
qRT-PCRReverse transcribe RNA to cDNA, then quantify PCR through fluorescenceSensitive targeted measurement; validate reference genes and amplification efficiency
ESTExpressed sequence tags: short sequence reads from cDNAHistorically useful for identifying expressed genes; incomplete transcript sampling
SAGESerial Analysis of Gene Expression; counts short transcript-derived tagsSequence tags represent expression; tag ambiguity and labour are limitations
MicroarrayHybridization to predefined probes on an arrayHigh throughput but depends on known sequences and suffers cross-hybridization / limited dynamic range
RNA-SeqSequence RNA-derived libraries (usually cDNA)Transcript discovery, quantification, isoforms and allele-specific expression


Microarray versus RNA-Seq
FeatureMicroarrayRNA-Seq
MeasurementProbe-hybridization intensitySequence reads / fragments
Prior knowledgePredefined probes requiredCan identify novel transcripts with suitable analysis
Dynamic rangeBackground and saturation can limit itTypically wider, but depends on depth and design
Isoforms / sequence variantsRestricted by probe designCan provide evidence for splicing and expressed variants
Main caveatCross-hybridization and probe biasMapping, library and sampling biases; computational demands
RNA-Seq is powerful, but cost and accuracy depend on the specific study. RNA-Seq variant detection is limited to expressed and covered regions and does not replace comprehensive DNA sequencing.


Noncoding RNAs are functional RNAs
RNARoleExample / detail
rRNAStructural and catalytic component of ribosomesParticipates in peptide-bond formation
tRNAAdaptor between codon and amino acidAnticodon pairs with mRNA
snRNAPre-mRNA splicingComponents of spliceosomal snRNPs
snoRNARNA processing and chemical modificationGuides rRNA modifications
miRNAPost-transcriptional regulationSmall RNAs guide Argonaute-containing complexes to targets, reducing translation and/or RNA stability
siRNASequence-directed gene silencingOften promotes cleavage of highly complementary target RNA
piRNATransposon silencing, especially in germ cellsAssociates with PIWI proteins
lncRNALong noncoding RNA, generally >200 nucleotidesCan regulate chromatin, transcription and RNA processing; XIST supports X-chromosome inactivation
Noncoding means it does not encode a protein; it does not mean biologically unimportant. Not every detected lncRNA has an established function. ncRNAs can act as regulators, guides, scaffolds or structural components.


Alternative splicing: one gene, multiple transcripts
Exons are joined after intron removal. Skipping exon 2 gives a different transcript isoform. Junction-spanning RNA-Seq reads provide evidence for these choices.
Bulk, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics
Bulk RNA-Seq measures the average profile of a mixed sample. Single-cell RNA-Seq separates cell profiles using cell-specific barcodes; UMIs can help count original molecules and reduce amplification bias. It identifies cell types and states but has sparse measurements, dropout and technical noise. Spatial transcriptomics preserves or reconstructs location, showing where transcriptional programmes occur in tissue.


Why bulk averages can hide biology
If a rare immune cell expresses a gene strongly, bulk data can dilute that signal. A change in the proportion of cell types can also look like a gene-regulation change even when expression within each cell type is unchanged.
Quick check · answer before revealing
1. Which method relies on predefined hybridization probes?
Probe design limits the sequences detectable by a microarray.
2. Which ncRNA participates in X-inactivation?
XIST is a well-known lncRNA.
3. Bulk RNA-Seq always distinguishes each cell type.
Bulk measures a mixed sample; single-cell approaches can resolve individual profiles.
Close the notes. Retrieve it.Contrast microarray and RNA-Seq. Write a 2.5-mark note on noncoding RNAs with at least three examples.

Teacher tutorial
9RNA-Seq: the complete analysis pipeline


Follow one question through the whole pipeline: which rice genes respond to heat stress, and which biological processes do they suggest?


Start with experimental design
Define the contrast, choose comparable tissue and collection time, include independent biological replicates, and randomize processing to avoid treatment being confounded with batch. Technical repeats assess measurement variability; they do not replace biological replication. More depth cannot rescue a design with no independent evidence about biological variation.


Your tutorial uses rice heat-stress data PRJNA597792, with three control and three treated examples. It also mentions a separate combined infection/temperature dataset PRJNA1039328. Keep these study accessions distinct.


Wet-lab generation
RNA extraction→Quality assessment→Poly(A) enrichment / rRNA depletion→cDNA synthesis→Fragmentation + adapters→Sequencing
Poly(A) selection enriches many mature eukaryotic mRNAs but excludes non-polyadenylated RNAs. rRNA depletion can retain a broader RNA population. Small-RNA sequencing needs an appropriate library protocol. Conventional RNA-Seq sequences cDNA; direct RNA sequencing is a distinct approach.


The computational route
01
Quality check
FASTQ → FastQC / MultiQC. Inspect base quality, adapters, duplication and sequence composition.
02
Preprocessing
fastp removes adapters and unsuitable reads. Recheck quality after processing.
03
Splice-aware alignment
HISAT2 maps to an indexed reference. SAM stores alignments; BAM is its compressed binary representation.
04
Quantification
featureCounts uses alignments + GTF gene models to assign reads/fragments to genes. Output: gene × sample count matrix.
05
Differential expression
DESeq2 estimates size factors and dispersion, fits a negative-binomial model and tests a specified contrast.
06
Functional interpretation
Visualize QC and changes; perform GO/pathway enrichment and network analysis; validate important targets.


featureCounts performs counting, not de novo transcript assembly. If there is no suitable reference, transcript assembly tools such as Trinity can assemble transcripts; this introduces different quantification and annotation challenges. Pseudoalignment/selective-alignment quantifiers provide another route to abundance estimation.


Understand the files
FormatContents / purpose
FASTQFour lines per read: @identifier, sequence, + separator, quality string
FASTA>identifier followed by sequence; no per-base quality string
SAM / BAMText / binary alignment records and alignment metadata
GTF / GFFGenomic feature coordinates and gene/transcript annotations
Count matrixRows = genes; columns = samples; raw assigned counts
DE results tableFold changes, uncertainty, test statistics and adjusted p-values
@read_001
ACGTACGT
+
IIIIIIII
The example quality string encodes scores, not nucleotide identities. In common Phred+33 encoding, I corresponds to Q40.


Phred quality, made concrete
Q = −10 log₁₀(Perror). Q20 means an error probability of 0.01 (1 in 100); Q30 means 0.001 (1 in 1,000), or 99.9% base-call accuracy. These are per-base error probabilities, not the percentage of reads that will map.




Normalization: why equal raw counts may mean unequal expression
A sample with twice the sequencing depth can produce about twice as many reads without a biological change. Longer transcripts can also attract more reads at the same molecule abundance. Normalization must fit the comparison being made.


MeasureFormula / ideaAppropriate interpretation
CPM / RPMcount ÷ total counts × 10⁶Library-size scaling; no gene-length correction
RPKMreads ÷ (gene length in kb × mapped reads in millions)Corrects length and library size for read-based abundance
FPKMfragments ÷ (length in kb × mapped fragments in millions)Fragment-based counterpart, commonly paired-end
TPMDivide counts by length first; scale the resulting rates to sum to 10⁶Length-normalized relative abundance; compositional, not absolute concentration
DESeq2 size factorsMedian-of-ratios scaling with model-based testingUse raw counts as input, with sample metadata and a design formula
Example: gene A has 100 reads and length 1 kb; B has 100 reads and length 2 kb. Length-adjusted rates are 100 and 50. In a two-gene toy sample their TPMs are about 666,667 and 333,333. Equal raw counts do not imply equal transcript concentration.


Do not feed TPM/FPKM into ordinary DESeq2
For the standard featureCounts → DESeq2 workflow, provide raw counts. DESeq2 performs its own normalization and models count variability. Gene-length correction is generally unnecessary when comparing the same gene across samples; it matters for comparisons among genes.


DESeq2 in the teacher’s terms
  1. Estimate sample size factors.
  2. Estimate gene-wise dispersion, describing variation beyond a Poisson count model.
  3. Fit the dispersion trend and shrink estimates for stability.
  4. Fit a generalized linear model (GLM) for each gene.
  5. Test the treatment contrast, often with a Wald test.
  6. Control multiple testing using Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-values.


ColumnMeaning
baseMeanMean normalized count across samples
log2FoldChangeLog₂ of the expression ratio for the defined contrast
lfcSEStandard error of the log₂ fold-change estimate
statTest statistic; commonly Wald
pvalueUnadjusted gene-level test p-value
padjP-value adjusted for multiple testing


log₂FC = +2 means fourfold higher expression; −2 means one-quarter as much, for treated/control. If the contrast is reversed, the signs reverse. A study may choose padj ≤ 0.05 and |log₂FC| ≥ 2 for a stringent set, but the effect-size threshold is a study choice.


Interpret a gene result
Illustrative rule: padj ≤ 0.05 and |log₂FC| ≥ 2.


A slide typo worth correcting
The tutorial’s significance slide has inconsistent inequality text. Upregulated under a ±2 cutoff means log₂FC ≥ +2; downregulated means log₂FC ≤ −2. Use adjusted p-values for the stated multiple-testing rule. The workshop’s example p<0.05 filters are not the same as FDR control.


Plots and biological interpretation
  • PCA: summarizes major variation; check sample clustering, outliers and possible batch effects.
  • Heatmap: displays relative expression patterns; scaling changes what colour means.
  • Volcano plot: effect size on x; −log₁₀ significance measure on y. Large effects and strong evidence are distinct.
  • MA plot: average abundance versus log fold change.
  • GO/pathway enrichment: asks whether functions/pathways occur more than expected relative to a suitable tested-gene background. Adjust enrichment p-values too.


Standards, reproducibility and EVORNA
MIAME = Minimum Information About a Microarray Experiment. MINSEQE = Minimum Information about a high-throughput Nucleotide SEQuencing Experiment; the lecture uses the phrase “Next-generation Sequencing Experiment”. Both emphasize experimental design, samples, protocols and processing so results can be interpreted and reproduced.
Computational pipeline: an automated series of tasks taking input data to output results. The EVORNA demonstration packages tools in Docker, mounts a working directory and runs a shell script. Inputs include BAMs, a GTF, sample information and an R analysis script; outputs include counts, QC/statistical plots and differential-expression CSVs. Docker helps preserve software environments; it does not correct bad biological design.
Optional hands-on vocabulary from the teacher’s workshop
ls       # list files
cd       # change directory
pwd      # print working directory
bash EVORNA.sh  # execute the workshop pipeline

R: library(DESeq2)  # load an installed package
A shell accepts commands; the operating-system kernel manages resources. A Docker image defines an environment; a container is a running instance. Mounting makes host files accessible in the container. Thread count controls parallel computational work. These are study examples; no installation is required to use this guide.
Quick check · answer before revealing
1. Q30 represents an error probability of…
Perror = 10^(−Q/10): Q30 = 0.001.
2. What goes into standard DESeq2 after featureCounts?
DESeq2 estimates its own size factors and models count variability.
3. log₂FC = −2 for treated/control means…
2^(−2) = 0.25: treated expression is one-quarter of control.
4. Under padj ≤ 0.05 and |log₂FC| ≥ 2, a gene with padj 0.08 and FC +3 passes.
The effect size passes but the adjusted significance criterion does not.
Close the notes. Retrieve it.Say the pipeline out loud using a file and tool at each stage. Explain Q30, raw counts, padj and a log₂FC of −2.

Review-paper theme
10Big data: promise, bottlenecks & computing


The bottleneck has shifted from generating data to moving, organizing, analysing and interpreting them reliably.


Biological big data are large, rapidly generated and heterogeneous datasets that strain ordinary workflows for storage, processing and interpretation. Size alone is not the definition; complexity and the resources needed to work with the data matter.


VMeaningBiological example
VolumeAmount of dataMillions of reads from many genomes
VelocityRate of generation / arrivalContinuous sequencing or sensor streams
VarietyDifferent formats and biological layersSequences, microscopy, EHR tables and text
VeracityReliability and uncertaintyErrors, incomplete metadata, batch effects
ValueUseful outcomes extractedValidated biomarkers or improved crop management
Structured data follow an explicit schema, like sample tables. Semi-structured data use tagged or flexible structure, such as JSON/XML or annotated records. Unstructured data include narrative text and images whose useful meaning is not already arranged in a conventional table.


Challenges paired with responses
ChallengeWhy it mattersResponse
Storage and growthData and backups accumulate faster than budgetsCompression, scalable storage, retention policies and backups
Transfer and accessBandwidth and download time can dominate analysisMove computation close to data; controlled APIs and cloud access
ComputeWhole datasets may not fit memory or a single machineParallel/distributed computing and efficient algorithms
HeterogeneityIdentifiers, units and experimental methods differStandards, ontologies, harmonization and curation
Quality / integrityNoise, corruption and missing labels undermine conclusionsQC, checksums, provenance, versioning and validation
ReproducibilityUndocumented settings and versions change outputsRecord pipelines, code, parameters, environments and metadata
Expertise and interpretationComputational output can be biologically misleadingCollaboration among biologists, statisticians and data scientists
Privacy and ownershipData can identify people or reveal commercial informationAppropriate access, consent and governance


Distributed computing without the jargon
Parallel computing divides work into tasks that run at the same time. Distributed computing spreads work over connected machines. Cloud computing provides computing/storage resources as services; cloud is not synonymous with a particular algorithm.
Hadoop combines distributed storage (HDFS) with processing frameworks such as MapReduce. MapReduce maps independent pieces of input to intermediate results, groups related results, then reduces them. Spark supports distributed analytics and can accelerate repeated operations through in-memory processing. GPU hardware is useful for suitable parallel numerical tasks. NoSQL systems offer alternatives such as document, key-value or graph models; they are not a guarantee of better performance for every task.


Read chunks→MAP: count bases in each→Group partial counts→REDUCE: add totals→Overall counts


Machine learning in biology
Supervised learning learns from labelled examples, such as known cancer subtypes. Unsupervised learning finds patterns without outcome labels, such as cell clusters. Deep learning uses multilayer neural networks and can learn complex representations from sequences or images.
Split data into training, validation and test sets appropriately. Related samples from the same patient/family must not leak across splits. Cross-validation helps estimate performance; external validation tests whether results generalize. High-dimensional omics often have many more variables than samples, making overfitting especially easy.


A memorable one-line conclusion
The promise of big data is improved discovery and prediction; the central challenge is converting large heterogeneous datasets into reliable, reproducible and biologically meaningful knowledge.
Quick check · answer before revealing
1. Veracity concerns…
The five Vs include reliability and uncertainty.
2. Putting related samples from one patient into train and test can cause…
Dependence across splits can inflate apparent performance.
Close the notes. Retrieve it.Name the five Vs. Pair four bottlenecks with a practical response. Explain MapReduce in one example.

Review-paper theme
11Data integration, FAIR & biocuration


Integration is more than putting files in one folder. The records must refer to the same entities, use compatible definitions, and support a meaningful comparison.


Three different integration problems
  • Technical/syntactic: formats, schemas, APIs and file conventions differ.
  • Semantic: words, gene identifiers and units may mean different things or use different names for the same thing.
  • Biological/statistical: assays measure different layers, scales, tissues and time points, with distinct errors and missing values.


A gene called “p14” may mean different genes in different contexts; a concentration in mg/L is not directly comparable with µg/mL until the units are reconciled. Linking identical text is not enough.


Infrastructure approaches
ApproachHow it worksTrade-off
Cross-links / indexingLink records using stable accessionsSimple navigation; depends on correct mapping
Data warehouseCopy and harmonize datasets in a central systemFast integrated analysis; updates and duplication must be managed
Federated queryQuery sources through common interfaces without one complete central copyUses distributed resources; availability and schema changes complicate queries
Semantic integrationUse controlled vocabulary, ontologies and explicit relationshipsImproves meaning; modelling and curation take effort


Multiomics: data-driven and knowledge-based approaches
The Noor paper distinguishes data-driven methods, which learn relationships from measurements, and knowledge-based methods, which use known interactions, pathways and mechanistic constraints.


StrategyExamplesStrength / limit
Statistical associationCorrelate RNA, protein and metabolite levels; molecular QTL analysisGenerates hypotheses rapidly; correlation does not establish causation
Unsupervised integrationPCA, clustering, matrix factorization, multiomics factor analysisFinds shared variation and cell states; factors require biological interpretation
Supervised integrationPredict phenotype from multiple omics layersUseful prediction; labels, overfitting and independent validation matter
Knowledge-based networks/modelsPathway networks, stoichiometric or kinetic metabolic modelsMechanistic interpretation; limited by prior knowledge and assumptions
In a metabolic pathway, enzyme amount, metabolite concentration and reaction rate are related but different quantities. A mechanistic model can encode stoichiometry and regulation; measuring more variables does not automatically identify every rate or causal mechanism.


Data-driven methods learn associations; knowledge-based models constrain them using known pathways and mechanisms. An integrated prediction still needs independent validation.
Ontologies and provenance
An ontology is a formal representation of concepts and their relationships. A controlled vocabulary standardizes terms. Gene Ontology (GO) describes molecular function, biological process and cellular component. Ontologies help computers interpret relationships; they are not just lists of gene names.
Provenance records where data came from and how they were transformed. Keep raw data, processing versions, parameters, sample identifiers and evidence links. A checksum can reveal accidental file corruption; a backup enables recovery. They solve different problems.


FAIR principles
LetterPrinciplePractical implementation
FFindableStable identifiers, rich metadata, searchable repositories
AAccessibleRetrievable through documented protocols, with authentication when needed
IInteroperableShared formats, ontologies and linked identifiers
RReusableClear licence, provenance, metadata and domain standards
FAIR does not mean all data must be openly downloadable. Controlled human-data access can still be FAIR when metadata and access procedures are clear.


Biocuration
Biocuration organizes and represents biological information so humans and computers can use it. Curators read literature, identify entities, extract experimental findings, attach evidence, standardize terms, resolve inconsistencies and maintain database records.


Publication / experiment→Identify entities→Extract findings→Standardize + annotate→Evidence & cross-links→Curated database
The Howe paper argues for collaboration among databases and journals, better reporting standards, and recognition/training/support for curators. Stable accessions, organism names and approved gene symbols help prevent ambiguity. Automated text mining can assist, but expert review remains important because context and evidence differ among papers.


Rice example
Combine heat-stress DEGs with protein measurements, metabolites and pathway annotations. Check that samples, gene identifiers and contrasts match. A coordinated response can suggest a stress pathway, but functional experiments are needed to test the proposed mechanism.
Quick check · answer before revealing
1. FAIR means every human dataset must be openly downloadable.
Accessible can include controlled access with documented procedures.
2. A gene-expression correlation proves direct regulation.
Correlation can suggest a hypothesis but not establish a direct causal edge.
3. A curator mainly…
Biocuration captures usable knowledge while preserving context and evidence.
Close the notes. Retrieve it.Explain why gene-name matching alone is insufficient. Recite FAIR and describe the job of a biocurator.

Review-paper theme
12Healthcare privacy, security & cognitive computing


Healthcare data can improve discovery and care while also revealing sensitive information about patients and their relatives.


Privacy versus security
Privacy concerns appropriate collection, use and disclosure of information, including expectations and control over access. Security protects systems and data from unauthorized access, alteration and loss. A well-secured system can still make an inappropriate use of data.


Security propertyMeaningExample
ConfidentialityOnly authorized parties access informationEncrypt data and restrict access
IntegrityInformation remains accurate and unaltered without authorizationChecksums, signatures and change controls
AvailabilityData and services are accessible when neededBackups, recovery plans and reliable infrastructure


Layered protection
  • Authentication: establish who the user is.
  • Authorization / access control: establish what that user may see or do; use minimum necessary access.
  • Encryption: protect data in transit and at rest; manage keys securely.
  • Masking/pseudonymization: replace identifying fields; retain a protected link when needed.
  • Monitoring and auditing: detect unusual access and document use.
  • Governance: define purposes, consent, access review and accountability.


Why removing names is insufficient
Age, postcode and sex can act as quasi-identifiers when linked with other information. Genomic data are particularly identifying and may reveal information about relatives. Pseudonymization replaces identifiers while a linkage remains possible; it is not equivalent to irreversible anonymization.


MethodMain ideaImportant limit
k-anonymityEach quasi-identifier combination occurs in at least k recordsSensitive values may still be inferred if a group is homogeneous
l-diversityRequire meaningful diversity of sensitive values within groupsDoes not remove every inference or background-knowledge risk
t-closenessKeep group sensitive-value distributions close to the overall distributionPrivacy can reduce data utility
Differential privacyBound how much an output changes when one individual’s data is includedNoise/privacy-budget choices affect usefulness
Secure computation / encryptionCompute or transmit while reducing exposure of dataCosts and assumptions vary by method


The ethical tension in the privacy paper
Privacy harms can be consequential, such as discrimination or stigma, or can concern an inappropriate loss of control even without a measurable downstream harm. Excessive restriction can also prevent valuable research and make datasets less representative. The task is accountable data stewardship that balances useful analysis, fairness, consent and context.
A learning health system routinely collects care data, analyses it and feeds findings back to improve care. Bias, validity, privacy and oversight matter at every stage. The uploaded articles discuss laws in their historical contexts; this guide teaches concepts rather than current legal compliance.


IBM Watson: the case study in your reading
The 2016 paper describes cognitive computing as a system that reads, reasons and learns from large, disparate data sources, especially unstructured scientific text. It combines natural-language processing, entity/relation extraction, evidence gathering and ranking to help researchers explore hypotheses and connections.


Literature & diverse data→Extract entities / relations→Generate candidate links→Evaluate evidence→Rank hypotheses→Human evaluation
Examples include connecting genes, diseases and drugs, prioritizing research targets and supporting literature-based discovery. Present these as applications described in the historical paper, not a claim about a currently available Watson product. Such systems can reflect biased or incomplete evidence and cannot replace biological validation or expert judgement.


Useful exam wording
Cognitive computing supports discovery by extracting and connecting information from large structured and unstructured datasets. Its usefulness depends on the quality, provenance and validation of the evidence.
Quick check · answer before revealing
1. A securely stored dataset used outside its agreed purpose may violate…
Security and appropriate use are distinct.
2. k-anonymity primarily groups records by…
Each quasi-identifier combination appears in at least k records.
3. Watson in the 2016 paper is best described as…
Its outputs require evidence assessment and validation.
Close the notes. Retrieve it.Explain how security can be strong while privacy is still violated. Contrast k-anonymity and differential privacy.

Applied review
13Big data for weed control & crop protection


A farmer needs an actionable decision: where are the weeds, what is the risk, and which treatment should be applied where?


The van Evert review groups data-intensive agriculture into farm management information systems (FMIS), precision agriculture, and automation/robotics. Precision agriculture manages spatial and temporal variability to improve returns and reduce environmental impact.


Cameras / drones / sensors→Weed, soil & weather data→Standardize locations + units→Predict / classify→Decision map→Targeted action→Measure outcome


Data and models
Inputs include crop/weed images, species observations, infestation maps, soil properties, weather, past treatments, yield maps and remote sensing. Regression can relate environmental variables to risk; support vector machines and neural networks can classify patterns; graphical models can represent dependencies and uncertainty.
For example, a camera detects weed patches and a spatial decision map guides targeted spraying. Weather and weed-development models can help choose timing. Predicted risk must be evaluated locally: lighting, season, field conditions and species differences can change performance.


Benefits and constraints
Potential benefitCondition required
Target treatment to infested areasAccurate detection, location and decision thresholds
Reduce unnecessary herbicide useValidate treatment effectiveness and environmental outcomes
Improve resistant/invasive weed managementReliable species/risk information and coordinated responses
Share learning across farmsCompatible metadata, units, semantics and agreed data rights
Challenges include fragmented sources, inconsistent units and meanings, missing data, uncertain model predictions, connectivity and costs. Farmers may be concerned about who owns data and who benefits from sharing. The review uses an ethical matrix to consider well-being, autonomy and justice for stakeholders such as farmers, agribusiness, consumers and the environment.


Do not skip interpretation
A high model accuracy on old images does not guarantee success on a new field. Evaluate predictions using representative data and connect them to a practical management decision.
Quick check · answer before revealing
1. Precision agriculture primarily manages…
It uses location- and time-specific information to improve decisions.
2. A weed classifier should be tested…
New seasons, lighting and field conditions can affect generalization.
Close the notes. Retrieve it.Give one end-to-end agricultural application and two data-sharing challenges.

Timed writing practice
90:00
  
Practise on paper, or type notes here. Notes are saved in this browser where supported.
Q1(a). Define bioinformatics and computational biology.
2 marks · model response
Bioinformatics is an interdisciplinary field that develops and applies computational tools for the collection, storage, retrieval, analysis and interpretation of biological data, such as DNA/protein sequences, structures and gene-expression data.
Computational biology applies mathematical, statistical and computational models to understand biological systems and test biological hypotheses, for example by modelling a gene regulatory network. The two fields overlap substantially.
Answer sheet 1 / 11
Q1(b). Provide an overview of the historical development of bioinformatics, highlighting key milestones and major advancements.
5 marks · model response
Bioinformatics developed through the combination of molecular biology, sequence analysis, databases and computing. Its major milestones are:
  1. 1953–1955: the DNA double-helix model and Sanger’s insulin sequence established the importance of molecular sequence information.
  2. 1965: Margaret Dayhoff’s Atlas of Protein Sequence and Structure systematized protein sequences and laid foundations for sequence databases.
  3. 1970–1971: Needleman–Wunsch enabled global sequence alignment, and the Protein Data Bank began archiving macromolecular structures.
  4. 1977: Sanger and Maxam–Gilbert DNA sequencing methods enabled direct determination of nucleotide sequences.
  5. 1980s: sequence archives such as GenBank expanded; Smith–Waterman local alignment, Swiss-Prot protein curation and the establishment of NCBI supported analysis and access.
  6. 1990: BLAST enabled fast database similarity searches, and the Human Genome Project began.
  7. 2001–2003: publication of the draft human genome and completion of the HGP provided a reference for comparative genomics and disease-gene research.
  8. 2005 onward: NGS and RNA-Seq increased throughput; multiomics, single-cell analysis and machine learning expanded biological interpretation.
Thus, the field progressed from analysing individual sequences to integrating genome-scale and systems-level biological data.
Answer sheet 2 / 11
Q1(c). Discuss the importance of bioinformatics in modern biology and medicine, with suitable examples.
3 marks · model response
Bioinformatics makes large biological datasets usable and supports discovery in biology and medicine.
  1. Genome analysis: sequence comparison and annotation identify genes and evolutionary relationships; for example, BLAST can identify a candidate homolog of an unknown sequence.
  2. Disease research and diagnosis: variant analysis links genomic changes with inherited disease, while RNA-Seq can identify gene-expression changes and potential biomarkers in cancer or stress responses.
  3. Drug discovery and precision medicine: protein structures, pathways and molecular profiles help prioritize drug targets and investigate why patients differ in treatment response.
Computational findings guide experiments and clinical research; important predictions require appropriate validation.
Answer sheet 3 / 11
Q2(a–c). What is data? What is a database? Describe the ways of classifying biological databases and explain each type with examples.
1 + 1 + 3 = 5 marks · model response
Data: recorded observations or measurements, such as a nucleotide sequence, a protein structure or a gene-expression value.
Database: an organized collection of related data, usually a computerized archive, stored so information can be retrieved, managed and updated efficiently.
Biological databases can be classified on several independent bases:
  1. By origin of information: primary databases store original experimental data, e.g. GenBank/DDBJ nucleotide sequences and PDB structures. Secondary databases store information derived by analysis of primary data, e.g. PROSITE motifs and SCOP/CATH structural classifications. Composite or integrated resources combine information from multiple sources, e.g. InterPro and GeneCards.
  2. By type of data: nucleotide sequences (GenBank), protein sequences (UniProt), motifs/families (PROSITE/Pfam), three-dimensional structures (PDB), gene-expression data (GEO), and pathways (KEGG).
  3. By availability/accessibility: resources may be publicly accessible, available under licence, academic/restricted, or proprietary/commercial. Human-data repositories may require controlled access.
These axes are complementary: a database can be a public primary nucleotide-sequence database at the same time.
Answer sheet 4 / 11
Q3(a–c). Full forms of NCBI and EBI; NCBI search engine; advanced PubMed literature-search options with examples.
1 + 1 + 3 = 5 marks · model response
NCBI: National Center for Biotechnology Information.
EBI: European Bioinformatics Institute.
The integrated search and retrieval system used at NCBI is Entrez.
PubMed supports advanced literature searches using:
  1. Boolean operators: AND combines concepts; OR combines synonyms; NOT excludes terms. Example: (asthma OR wheeze) AND child.
  2. Field-specific searching: restrict terms to title/abstract [tiab], author [au], MeSH [mh] or publication date [dp]. Example: BRCA1[tiab].
  3. MeSH terms: controlled vocabulary improves retrieval of indexed concepts. Combine MeSH with keywords to include newer records.
  4. Advanced Search Builder and history: construct field-based searches, combine sets such as #1 AND #2, and inspect Search Details.
  5. Filters: refine by date, article type, language or species, while considering possible exclusion of incompletely indexed records.
For example:
("Breast Neoplasms"[mh] OR "breast cancer"[tiab])
AND BRCA1[tiab] AND review[pt]
This combines a disease concept, a gene keyword and a review publication type.
Answer sheet 5 / 11
Q4. List five computational tools, software or algorithms used in bioinformatics and explain their specific applications.
1 × 5 = 5 marks · model response
  1. BLAST: searches sequence databases for local similarity; used to identify candidate homologs of an unknown DNA or protein sequence.
  2. ClustalW: performs multiple sequence alignment; used to detect conserved residues or motifs within a protein family.
  3. MEGA: supports molecular evolutionary analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction; used to study relationships among organisms or genes.
  4. HISAT2: performs splice-aware read alignment; used to map RNA-Seq reads to a reference genome, including exon-junction reads.
  5. DESeq2: models count data and tests differential expression; used to identify genes whose expression differs between treated and control samples.
Answer sheet 6 / 11
Q5(a). Short note: Human Genome Project.
2.5 marks · model response
The Human Genome Project (HGP) was an international research effort conducted from 1990 to 2003 to determine a human reference genome sequence and map genes. It also advanced sequencing technology, computational analysis, public data sharing and study of ethical, legal and social issues.
The draft sequence was published in 2001, and completion was announced in April 2003. The human genome contains approximately 3 billion base pairs.
The HGP provided a foundation for comparative genomics, identifying disease-associated variants and future precision-medicine research. The original reference still contained gaps and did not establish the function of every genomic element.
Answer sheet 7 / 11
Q5(b). Short note: Next Generation Sequencing.
2.5 marks · model response
Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) comprises high-throughput technologies that sequence large numbers of DNA fragments in parallel. It greatly increases throughput and reduces cost per base compared with traditional Sanger sequencing.
A typical workflow is:
DNA/cDNA→Library + adapters→Parallel sequencing→Reads→Analysis
For example, Illumina uses sequencing by synthesis, with fluorescent nucleotide incorporation and repeated imaging. NGS is used for whole-genome and exome sequencing, RNA-Seq, variant detection and metagenomics.
Limitations include sequencing/mapping errors, uneven coverage, computational demands and difficulties interpreting variants.
Answer sheet 8 / 11
Q5(c). Short note: Noncoding RNAs.
2.5 marks · model response
Noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) are functional RNA molecules that do not encode proteins. They perform structural, catalytic and regulatory roles.
  1. rRNA and tRNA participate in translation; rRNA forms key ribosomal components and tRNA carries amino acids.
  2. snRNA and snoRNA are involved in splicing and RNA modification.
  3. miRNA regulates target mRNAs through repression and/or degradation.
  4. lncRNA, generally longer than 200 nucleotides, can regulate chromatin and gene expression; XIST is involved in X-chromosome inactivation.
Thus, RNA is not merely an intermediate between DNA and protein.
Answer sheet 9 / 11
Q5(d). Short note: Genome India Project.
2.5 marks · model response
GenomeIndia is a Department of Biotechnology-supported initiative launched in 2020 to catalogue genetic variation among India’s diverse populations.
Its initial phase sequenced approximately 10,000 individuals from 99 communities to build an Indian population genomic resource. The data resource was dedicated to researchers in January 2025.
It supports population genetics, interpretation of genetic variants, disease research and future precision-medicine approaches. Representative sampling, consent and protection of genomic data are important. It is a population resource rather than a project to sequence every Indian citizen.
Answer sheet 10 / 11
Q5(e). Short note: ENCODE project.
2.5 marks · model response
ENCODE stands for ENCyclopedia Of DNA Elements. Launched in 2003, it aims to identify functional elements in the human genome.
It maps features such as coding and noncoding transcripts, promoters, enhancers, transcription-factor binding sites and chromatin states using high-throughput assays and computational analysis.
The HGP provided a reference sequence; ENCODE helps interpret how that sequence is regulated and used in different cell types. Its data support research on gene regulation and disease-associated variants. Biochemical activity alone does not establish that every active base is essential.
Answer sheet 11 / 11

Where the material comes from
The lessons synthesize the examinable concepts and major themes across all 22 supplied PDFs, rather than reproducing every article, reference or workshop command. The two Watson PDFs contain identical extracted text and are treated as one reading. The photographed PYQ determines the explicit model-answer set.
The guide retains course terminology such as firing a query, high-throughput, omics, cross-referencing, differential expression, systems approaches and the named tools in the teacher’s tutorial. Explanations and answers are newly written. Instructions found inside readings are treated as source content, not commands to perform.

Clarifications to older notes
  • PDB establishment: 1971; Swiss-Prot: 1986; GenBank official start: 1982. Earlier collection work and later announcements can cause date confusion.
  • GenBank is principally a nucleotide-sequence archive; protein translations may be included in annotations.
  • Crick’s rule concerns sequence information leaving protein, so reverse transcription does not violate it.
  • DNA base pairs use hydrogen bonds: A–T has two and G–C three. Nucleotide incorporation is catalysed by polymerases using nucleoside triphosphates; ATP does not simply “add bases”.
  • Transcription is DNA → RNA; translation is RNA → protein. RNA replication uses RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
  • featureCounts counts features; it does not assemble a transcriptome.
  • The tutorial’s ±2 differential-expression thresholds require ≥+2 for upregulation and ≤−2 for downregulation. Multiple testing is addressed with adjusted p-values.
  • Platform read lengths, error rates, prices and older database-release numbers are historical snapshots.
  • MIAME and MINSEQE are reporting standards, not analysis software. The standard MINSEQE expansion differs slightly from the lecture wording.
Sources were reviewed and clarifications checked on 6 October 2026. External links are optional references: they are not needed for the lessons, quizzes, diagrams, fonts or answers.
